newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech govt to curb rising municipal debt - minister.
newsitem.headline: Czech govt to curb rising municipal debt - minister.

text.p: The Czech government on Tuesday said it plans to curb local authorities's growing penchant for borrowing, after municipal indebtedness rose to record levels in 1996.

Transport Minister Martin Riman told a news conference following a ministers meeting that some small villages have taken on an "unreasonable and unhealthy" debt burden, forcing the government to take steps to control borrowing.
"(Participants of) the meeting agreed that the state should find instruments, both technical and legislative, to set limits for municipalities' debts," said Riman.

Many towns and villages took bank loans or issued bonds in the past years to finance development projects pushing municipal indebtedness to over 30 billion crowns by the end of 1996, up from just seven billion in 1993.
Riman said the government should require local administrations to conduct audits of their budgets, which would be checked by the state before it grants state subsidies.

He said the proposed measures included banning local authorities by law from providing guarantees on loans to entrepreneurs, or raising the proportion of votes needed for passing municipal council decisions concerning property transfers.
The Czech centre-right government has made healthy public finances a cornerstone of its policies, achieving four consecutive balanced state budgets. It also approved a balanced budget for 1997.
